title: The one Giver
hook: the Giver alone gives; all others are passing (Sukhmani 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, don't lean on mortals, and your line: lean on the one. Did you forgive someone for being human? Today the same stanza names the One you lean on: the Giver. Day four hundred ninety-two.
screen: `DON'T LEAN ON MORTALS — LEAN ON THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Pick up whatever you ate last. A piece of toast, say. Who gave you that? The store, sure. But the store got it from a bakery, the bakery from a mill, the mill from a farm. The farmer planted, but didn't make the seed grow, or the rain fall, or the sun rise. Follow any gift back far enough and the chain of hands gets very long, and then it runs out of hands. Sukhmani has a name for what's at the end of the chain. Today: the one Giver.
screen: `WHO GAVE YOU THE TOAST?` → `STORE, BAKERY, MILL, FARM.` → `THE CHAIN RUNS OUT OF HANDS.`

segments.voice: The fourteenth ashtpadi's first stanza, which yesterday warned against leaning on mortals, goes on in paraphrase: the Giver is the One Lord alone. By whose gift a person is satisfied, and thirst does not come back to cling to them. Look at that second half, because it's the real point. There are two kinds of giving in this stanza. One kind fills you for a moment and leaves you hungrier: the raise that makes you want a bigger raise, the praise that makes you need more praise. The other kind leaves you satisfied, aghaai, full, with the thirst gone. Sukhmani says only the One gives the second kind. The Giver has come up much earlier on this path. In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak asks the Guru for one understanding, and it's this: there is one Giver of all beings; may I never forget Him. Daataa, in Punjabi. The Giver. It's an everyday name for God in Sikh speech. People can thank the Giver in passing, in a word or two, when the crops come in, when the baby is born, when the test results are good. Now notice what that does to every other gift. Your boss, your parents, the farmer, the stranger who held the door: they're real, and they deserve real thanks. But in this picture they're hands in the chain, not the source. Their gifts pass through them. That's not an insult to them. It's a relief. Nobody has to be the bottom of your well. And everything given to you, from the toast to the breath you just took, is a thread you can follow back to the same place.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF GIVING.` · `AGHAAI: FULL, AND THE THIRST GONE.` · `DAATAA: THE GIVER, IN JAPJI.` · `EVERY HAND A LINK IN THE CHAIN.` · then, large: `ONE GIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: follow one gift back. Choose one thing you have right now: the water you drank, the clothes you're wearing, the breath in your chest. Trace it back, hand by hand, as far as you can. Thank each hand quietly as you pass it. When you run out of hands, stop, and rest there a moment. If you pray, you can thank the one Giver in whatever words are yours. The bell holds the time.
The one Giver. Daataa: the Giver whose gift leaves you full, with the thirst gone; every other giver is a hand in the chain.
Your line: one giver. Today, when you thank someone, thank them fully, and then let the thanks travel one step further back. Day four hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs call God daataa, the Giver, in daily speech and in Gurbani; Japji Sahib asks never to forget the one Giver of all beings, and Sukhmani's fourteenth ashtpadi names the Giver whose gift satisfies.

myth: the stanza says some gifts leave you thirstier, and the One's gift ends the thirst
by the One's gift a person stays satisfied, and thirst does not cling again.
seeing God as the one Giver means people deserve no thanks
people are real hands in the chain and deserve real thanks; they're just not the source.
daataa is a rare, formal word for God
it's an everyday name for God, in Gurbani and in Sikh speech.

fork.setup: you just got a raise. a week later you already want a bigger one. what kind of gift was it, in the fourteenth ashtpadi's terms?
options: a gift that ends the thirst.
a gift that leaves the thirst behind.
fork.reveal: a real gift, through real hands, but one that leaves thirst. the stanza says only the One's gift leaves a person satisfied.

original.note: Gurmukhi: daataa, the Giver, a common name for God in Gurbani and Sikh speech.

trapdoor: what you thought: God gives, so ask God for stuff.
what it means: every gift passes through many hands from one source, and only that source's gift ends the thirst.
what a scholar hears: the stanza's aghaai, sated, sits beside trisnaa, craving, a core Gurbani theme; Japji pauri 5 asks never to forget the one daataa.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 14, stanza 1 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 281)

notes: Ashtpadi 14 stanza 1 lines paraphrased: devan kau ekai bhagvaan; jis kai deeai rahai aghaai, bahur na trisnaa laagai aai. Confirm.
Japji: sabhnaa jeeaa kaa ik daataa so mai visar na jaaee, in pauri 5 (and repeated in pauri 6): confirm.
